briefing.title: We must defend our widening coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend reporting allegations about a prominent university appointment, while preserving the distinction between questions and findings. Our first listed report, on the first of August, put Arday’s defence in its headline. It described the source of the allegations and carried opposing academic views. But its wording about not disputing allegations deserves scrutiny alongside his later explicit denial. We cannot let repeated reporting flatten those distinctions.

After his resignation on the fifth, our coverage continued into institutional responses. Our analysis the next day connected appointment checks with diversity policy, while also carrying the union’s counterargument. On the tenth, we reported a cancelled appearance and another association resignation, and checked other roles. By the twelfth, an independent appointment inquiry supplied a further development. These were different developments, but that does not automatically justify every part of the follow-up.

We owe you an answer about proportion. Nine written pieces are listed, with two on each of our busiest dates. Our first report had already carried a warning about the effect of continuing scrutiny. Arday later described the toll on his family. What public need did tracking the remaining roles serve, and could we have explained institutional responsibility with less personal exposure? Those are fair challenges to our editorial choices.

The earlier O’Reilly complaint also tests consistency. Its quieter coverage is a columnist’s estimate, not a matched census. And our nine written pieces exclude broadcasts; they cannot be compared directly with a broader pages-and-programmes tally. We would need a complete record of our attention and significant edits to defend the campaign as a whole.

briefing.title: We investigated claims and challenged the wider backlash

paragraphs.text: We would defend this campaign as both investigation and a debate about its wider consequences. On the first of August, reporting questioned accounts of alleged racist threats. Four days later, Arday resigned from Cambridge. He denied plagiarism and said stepping down was not acceptance of the narratives about him. Those responses matter alongside the allegations.

Eighteen of our pieces are listed. There were four on the sixth of August, four the following day and another four on the twelfth, when the appointment inquiry was announced. Selected opinion headlines defended diversity. Our case is that readers needed both scrutiny of the university and a challenge to arguments treating one contested case as a verdict on racial equality.

But that does not make every additional piece necessary. Investigations, opinion columns and letters all add to the attention focused on the same person. Even supportive commentary can prolong that spotlight. We must defend the amount of new understanding our campaign offered, as well as the merits of any one article.

A quieter Cambridge case gives you a question to put to us. Varsity reported that a plagiarism complaint against historian William O’Reilly was upheld, with a negligence finding, and that he returned to work. A columnist estimated much less press coverage. We cannot dismiss the consistency question. But we also cannot turn that rough estimate into a proven comparison: there is no matching inventory, and the cases were at different stages. Ask us why those differences would justify the scale of attention here.

briefing.title: We treated this as an argument about institutional standards

paragraphs.text: Our defence starts with Cambridge, rather than a final finding against Arday. An early commentary on the thirtieth of July acknowledged that the plagiarism question remained unresolved. It challenged the university’s appointment checks. We would argue that an institution’s decisions deserve scrutiny while allegations against an individual are still being examined.

Then the campaign broadened. Five of our pieces are listed on the fifth of August, the date Arday resigned. Our leading article argued that the affair exposed wider problems with academic standards and progressive politics. Five more pieces are listed on the tenth. One commentary used fictional impostors to make an argument against diversity, equity and inclusion. That was political opinion; it was not a new tribunal finding.

Twenty-one pieces are listed altogether, with ten concentrated on those two dates. We would defend commentary that explains why a university controversy matters beyond one appointment. But we owe you evidence for that wider argument. One contested case cannot establish the merit of whole groups, and repeating a political judgment does not make it better supported.

Arday denied plagiarism and said scrutiny had taken a toll on his family. Your challenge to us is whether this intensity kept adding something the public needed, or whether our commentary became a succession of opportunities to rehearse the same argument at his expense.

The O’Reilly comparison can test consistency, but its quieter coverage is a columnist’s estimate, not an equivalent article count. It should prompt a question to us, rather than decide the answer for you.

briefing.title: We kept asking questions after the resignation

paragraphs.text: We would defend sustained attention because resignation did not answer the questions about Cambridge’s appointment or the accuracy of public claims. Our first listed report appeared on the twenty-fourth of July, framing a plagiarism row around a much-publicised appointment. Later headings moved into Arday’s memoir, the university’s hiring decisions and wider political criticism. That widening agenda is central to the case you should put to us.

Arday resigned on the fifth of August. He denied plagiarism and said scrutiny had taken a toll on his family. The next two dates were our busiest: seven listed pieces on the sixth and seven on the seventh. Thirty pieces fall on or after the resignation date. The archive lists forty-two altogether, making this the most sustained campaign among the four outlets in this round.

Our argument is that public claims and institutional responsibility can remain news after a person leaves their job. But that is a reason to investigate further, not a blank cheque for the volume we published. You should ask which later pieces uncovered something important, which explained developments, and which mainly repeated an established criticism. The listed headings suggest different themes, but cannot prove that every article added fresh evidence.

A comparison with William O’Reilly raises the question of consistency. Varsity documented an upheld complaint, a negligence finding and a withdrawn article. A columnist described much quieter attention, without a matching count or period. We would have to explain why the differences between the cases warranted our intensity here. We cannot simply say that a serious allegation makes any amount of coverage proportionate.

title: Caroline Flack: six months of press coverage
subject: Caroline Flack coverage by The Sun within the Guardian’s six-month print analysis
endNote: The Guardian’s analysis window ends on 14 February 2020; exact inclusion-time convention is not stated.
dataCompleteness: One outlet aggregate from a bounded six-month print-media analysis; no daily series or item-level corpus is available here.

source.name: The Guardian analysis
source.unit: print stories in which Caroline Flack appeared in the headline or body
source.scopeNote: The Guardian reports 387 print stories across UK national newspapers for 14 Aug 2019–14 Feb 2020, including 99 mentioning Flack in The Sun. Inclusion means her name in the headline or body. This is an aggregate only: outlet universe is not itemized here, and no daily counts, active days, peak, before/after split or complete headline corpus is supplied. Three journalists categorized stories by tone; the Guardian calls the analysis non-definitive. The 99 are not all established as negative, and this record does not claim the coverage caused her death. The example is an online Sun story, reported by The Independent, and is not verified as one of the 99 print-corpus items. This method is not comparable to a census of distinct substantive online articles.

evidence.label: Guardian aggregate and method
evidence.text: The Guardian reports 387 print stories across UK national newspapers and 99 Sun stories mentioning Flack. Inclusion was her name in headline or body during 14 Aug 2019–14 Feb 2020. Three journalists classified tone; the article says the analysis is not definitive. Most stories were neutral overall; December negative headlines rose to 35% versus 18% positive, while February had equal positive and negative counts.

evidence.label: Charge report, 13 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack was charged with assault by beating on 13 December after an incident the previous day. The allegation was not a conviction.

evidence.label: Flack steps down from Love Island, 17 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV reported that Flack stood down from the upcoming series after the charge. Her statement said reports about her private life did not reflect events as she understood them; she said she would cooperate with authorities and could not comment further during the legal process. ITV accepted her decision.

evidence.label: Laura Whitmore named host, 20 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV announced Laura Whitmore as the replacement host after Flack stepped down; Whitmore described Flack as a friend and said she wished circumstances were better.

evidence.label: Not-guilty plea reported, 24 December 2019
evidence.text: ITV’s 24 December report states Flack pleaded not guilty at Highbury Corner Magistrates’ Court on 23 December. She remained on bail ahead of a trial then scheduled for March. The same report records her statement that scrutiny and speculation were difficult to face alone and that she was taking time away to feel better.

evidence.label: Reported headline of removed Sun online story
evidence.text: The Independent reported that The Sun published an online story on 14 February about a Valentine card mocking Flack in relation to the alleged assault; it reproduced the headline excerpt “Brutal Caroline Flack Valentine’s Day card mocks troubled star”. This confirms an online story, not its presence in the Guardian’s print corpus.

evidence.label: Removal reported after the window
evidence.text: By Saturday evening, 15 February, the online story had been replaced with a legal removal notice. The Guardian says the exact removal time was unclear, so the record does not establish whether removal preceded or followed the public announcement. This is outside the print-count window.

evidence.label: Public debate about press coverage
evidence.text: The Guardian reported criticism of tabloid coverage and recorded The Sun executive editor Dan Wootton’s public claim that ITV had failed to stand by Flack. The response and criticism are viewpoints, not evidence that coverage caused her death.

briefing.title: A difficult story, and a harder editorial question

paragraphs.text: We covered a presenter whose private life became public through a criminal charge and her departure from a major television programme. Caroline Flack was charged with assault by beating on 13 December 2019. Four days later she stepped down from Love Island, saying reports about her were inaccurate and she could not comment during the legal process. She pleaded not guilty on 23 December. Neither is a verdict.

A published press review raises a serious question about scale: 99 print stories mentioning Flack in our paper, within 387 across UK national newspapers from 14 August 2019 to 14 February 2020. The rule covered her name in headline or body. This is not 99 headlines or negative stories. The review found mixed tone overall and supplies no daily values or complete outlet item list.

One difficult example is our online story, reported on the fourteenth of February, about a Valentine card joking about the alleged assault. This followed Flack’s public account in December of the strain of scrutiny and speculation. We can identify the story and its later removal, but cannot link it to the 99 print entries. Did highlighting the card inform readers or turn an unresolved allegation into mockery? We owe you a justification for that choice.

We would need to explain whether we treated comparable public figures consistently. This record has no matched case or item-level archive, so we cannot make that comparison or say what each story added. Reporting a charge and programme change had public value; that does not justify every follow-up. The total establishes volume, not that all 99 were hostile, that editors intended harm, or that coverage caused Flack’s death.
